---
title: "From VALEX distributions to MegaAcceptability profiles"
---

Can a compressed summary of a verb's corpus frame distribution predict its
acceptability profile better than the complete distribution? We compare two
procedures on verbs excluded from fitting. The direct procedure uses every
VALEX frame proportion; the compressed procedure replaces those proportions
with a smaller set of directions estimated from the training verbs. Both
procedures predict the same MegaAcceptability response profiles with the same
regression model, so their held-out difference isolates the proposed
compression.

[VALEX](https://ilexir.co.uk/valex/) was acquired automatically from five corpora and the Web. Korhonen, Krymolowski, and Briscoe's [dataset paper](https://www.cs.brandeis.edu/~marc/misc/proceedings/lrec-2006/pdf/558_pdf.pdf) describes counts for English verb subcategorization frames and emphasizes automatic acquisition. The counts may contain parsing and frame-assignment error, and the release does not disambiguate verb senses.

[MegaAcceptability](https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-acceptability/) contains judgments for English clause embedding verbs in semantically bleached frames. [White and Rawlins (2020)](https://doi.org/10.5334/gjgl.1001) constructed lists in which each verb and frame appeared at most once, collected ordinal responses from participants reporting native American English, and modeled the relation between corpus frequencies and acceptability. We retain their held out verb target and compare raw VALEX proportions with a PCA representation while holding the predictive model fixed.

The remaining questions are concrete. What does one row from each resource
measure? How do the direct and compressed procedures turn those rows into
predictions without using a held-out verb? And which procedure predicts those
verbs more accurately?

## What the VALEX and MegaAcceptability rows record {#valex-megaacceptability-data}

The retained overlap contains one VALEX row per matched verb and one MegaAcceptability response profile per matched verb. If $c_{vj}$ is the automatically acquired count for verb $v$ in VALEX dimension $j$, define the within-verb proportion

$$
p_{vj}
=
\frac{c_{vj}}{\sum_h c_{vh}}.
$$

The row $\mathbf p_v$ records how automatically extracted corpus evidence for verb form $v$ is allocated across frames after division by that verb's total extracted count. This normalization removes the total-frequency scale, and the release does not disambiguate senses or turn parser assignments into grammatical descriptions.

The raw MegaAcceptability unit is one participant's ordinal response to one
verb-frame item. The following arithmetic treats the seven ordered response
categories as if equal numerical steps represented equal changes in
acceptability: it subtracts a mean, divides by a standard deviation, and later
averages. That interval-scale working assumption makes these operations
available, but the recorded order alone does not establish it. Within a training
set $\mathcal T$, participant $q$'s response is transformed as

$$
z_{qi}
=
\frac{y_{qi}-\bar y_{q,\mathcal T}}
     {s_{q,\mathcal T}}.
$$

These values are averaged within verb-frame cells to form a response matrix
\(\mathbf Y\) with one verb per row and one experimental frame per column.
These are empirical averages of recorded responses; the [expected-value
page](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd) instead defines
an average under a probability model. Zero marks a participant's
training-fitted mean on this transformed coordinate. Because the task supplied
ordered acceptability responses rather than a grammaticality cutoff, no
transformation step makes zero a boundary between grammatical and ungrammatical
sentences. This transformation is a fold-fitted approximation to the paper's
ordinal normalization.

The raw course bundle retains the verb, schematic experimental frame, participant,
and numeric response, but not the fully lexicalized sentence string or the wording
of the scale endpoints. We thus do not invent either. The recorded response scale
runs from 1 to 7, with larger values treated as greater acceptability. The frame
notation is read compositionally: `NP` is a noun phrase, `S` a finite clause, `VP`
a verb phrase, `Ved` the target verb in past-tense form, and bracketed material
marks a controlled semantic or morphosyntactic feature.

## What information do the two procedures need?

For every held-out verb-by-frame cell, we need four quantities: the observed
MegaAcceptability profile value, the training-frame-mean baseline, the
prediction from the complete VALEX distribution, and the prediction from its
compressed representation. To reconstruct those predictions, we also need the
raw VALEX counts by verb and frame, the participant response rows, and the
training split in which each normalization, component direction, rank, and
penalty was estimated.

::: {.callout-note title="Reproducibility files"}
The course bundle stores the source counts and responses together with the
fold-level predictions, validation curves, and declared summary files under
`data/valex-megaacceptability/audited`. The code below reads those records and
recomputes the displayed checks; the later fitting section shows how the
predictions are obtained from a training split.
:::

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

analysis_root <- "data/valex-megaacceptability/audited"
valex <- read.csv(
  gzfile(file.path(analysis_root, "valex-counts.csv.gz")),
  check.names = FALSE
)
mega <- read.csv(
  gzfile(file.path(analysis_root, "megaacceptability-responses.csv.gz")),
  check.names = FALSE
)
outer <- read.csv(
  gzfile(file.path(analysis_root, "outer-predictions.csv.gz")),
  check.names = FALSE
)
inner <- read.csv(
  gzfile(file.path(analysis_root, "inner-validation-curves.csv.gz")),
  check.names = FALSE
)
family_metrics <- read.csv(
  file.path(analysis_root, "family-metrics.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
pilot_summary <- jsonlite::read_json(
  file.path(analysis_root, "pilot-summary.json"),
  simplifyVector = TRUE
)

count_matrix <- as.matrix(valex[-1])
P <- count_matrix / rowSums(count_matrix)
rownames(P) <- valex$verb

stopifnot(
  all(abs(rowSums(P) - 1) < 1e-12),
  setequal(unique(mega$verb), valex$verb),
  length(unique(mega$frame)) == length(unique(outer$frame)),
  all(c("outcome", "baseline", "direct", "factor") %in% names(outer))
)

c(
  matched_verbs = nrow(P),
  VALEX_dimensions = ncol(P),
  experimental_frames = length(unique(mega$frame)),
  raw_responses = nrow(mega),
  participants = length(unique(mega$participant))
)
```

The empirical objects contain `r nrow(P)` matched verbs, `r ncol(P)` observed VALEX dimensions, `r length(unique(mega$frame))` experimental frames, and `r format(nrow(mega), big.mark = ",")` retained responses from `r length(unique(mega$participant))` participants.

The verb *accept* supplies a concrete cross-resource record.

```{r}
accept_counts <- data.frame(
  verb = "accept",
  VALEX_frame = c("(VSUBCAT NP)-7", "(VSUBCAT SCOMP)-26"),
  gloss = c(
    "verb with a noun-phrase complement",
    "verb with a finite sentential complement"
  ),
  count = c(
    valex[valex$verb == "accept", "(VSUBCAT NP)-7"],
    valex[valex$verb == "accept", "(VSUBCAT SCOMP)-26"]
  )
)

accept_items <- mega |>
  dplyr::filter(verb == "accept") |>
  dplyr::slice(1:2)

example_response <- accept_items |>
  dplyr::slice(1)
participant_rows <- mega |>
  dplyr::filter(participant == example_response$participant)
participant_mean_example <- mean(participant_rows$response)
participant_sd_example <- sqrt(mean(
  (participant_rows$response - participant_mean_example)^2
))
example_response$illustrative_within_participant_z <-
  (example_response$response - participant_mean_example) /
  participant_sd_example

example_cell <- mega |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    illustrative_z = ave(
      response,
      participant,
      FUN = function(x) (x - mean(x)) / sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2))
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(
    verb == example_response$verb,
    frame == example_response$frame
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    verb = dplyr::first(verb),
    frame = dplyr::first(frame),
    participant_responses = dplyr::n(),
    illustrative_aggregated_z = mean(illustrative_z)
  )

knitr::kable(accept_counts)
knitr::kable(accept_items)
knitr::kable(example_response)
knitr::kable(example_cell)
```

The first table gives two observed corpus counts: one nominal-complement frame and
one finite-clause frame. The second gives two observed MegaAcceptability item
schemas and their raw participant responses. The third shows the arithmetic of
within-participant normalization for one recorded response, and the fourth averages
those normalized responses into one verb-by-frame target cell. These illustrative
normalizations use the full retained bundle only to expose the data ladder; the
actual evaluation refits each participant's origin and scale inside the relevant
training split.

Every retained verb has a response in every one of the 50 experimental frame
columns after aggregation, so the course outcome matrix has no missing verb-frame
cells. VALEX zeros are observed automatic counts rather than missing values. The
information removed by aggregation is participant-level variation, item-list
variation, and the ordinal response distribution within a verb-frame cell. We
aggregate because the target is multivariate held-out-verb prediction;
a participant-by-item model would preserve more variation and answer a richer
measurement question.

## Stating the competing procedures

The direct multivariate ridge model uses the complete VALEX proportion matrix. With an unpenalized intercept implemented by training centering, it solves

$$
(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{0,\lambda},
 \widehat{\mathbf B}_{\lambda})
=
\arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta_0,\mathbf B}
\left\|\mathbf Y_{\mathcal T}
-\mathbf 1\boldsymbol\beta_0^{\mathsf T}
-\mathbf P_{\mathcal T}\mathbf B\right\|_F^2
+\lambda\|\mathbf B\|_F^2.
$$

After centering predictors and outcomes, write the objective as

$$
Q(\mathbf B)
=
\|\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\mathbf B\|_F^2
+\lambda\|\mathbf B\|_F^2.
$$

The cells of \(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\mathbf B\) are [regression
residuals](../regression-models/residuals.qmd), observed response-profile values
minus their fitted values. The validation score later evaluates the same kind
of discrepancy on verbs that did not determine \(\mathbf B\).

To obtain the coefficient solution, recall that a
[derivative](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd#derivatives-as-local-rates-of-change)
measures how a criterion changes after a small parameter move. For one outcome
column \(\mathbf y\) and coefficient vector \(\mathbf b\), differentiating
\(\|\mathbf y-\mathbf X\mathbf b\|^2+\lambda\|\mathbf b\|^2\) gives
\(-2\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\mathbf b)+2\lambda\mathbf b\).
The **matrix derivative** stacks that same gradient across all outcome columns;
its \((j,k)\) cell is the derivative with respect to coefficient \(B_{jk}\).
Thus

$$
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial\mathbf B}
=
-2\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\mathbf B)
+2\lambda\mathbf B.
$$

Setting every cell of this derivative to zero gives the multivariate version of
the [normal equations](../regression-models/design-matrices.qmd#from-squared-error-to-the-coefficient-estimates):

$$
(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X+\lambda\mathbf I)\widehat{\mathbf B}
=
\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf Y,
$$

and thus

$$
\widehat{\mathbf B}_{\lambda}
=
(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X+\lambda\mathbf I)^{-1}
\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf Y.
$$

If \(\mathbf X=\mathbf U\mathbf D\mathbf V^{\mathsf T}\), substitution yields

$$
\widehat{\mathbf B}_{\lambda}
=
\mathbf V
\operatorname{diag}\left(
\frac{d_k}{d_k^2+\lambda}
\right)
\mathbf U^{\mathsf T}\mathbf Y.
$$

This is the code path in `ridge_prediction()`: `component_outcome` is
\(\mathbf U^{\mathsf T}\mathbf Y\), `shrinkage` stores
\(d_k/(d_k^2+\lambda)\), and the test scores supply
\(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{test}}\mathbf V\). Increasing \(\lambda\) shrinks weak
singular directions more strongly.

The factor procedure fits [principal component
analysis](principal-component-analysis.qmd#beginning-with-variation-around-column-means)
only to training predictor rows,

$$
\mathbf F_K
=
(\mathbf P-\mathbf 1\bar{\mathbf p}_{\mathcal T}^{\mathsf T})
\mathbf V_{\mathcal T,K},
$$

then substitutes $\mathbf F_K$ for $\mathbf P$ in the same ridge objective. The outcomes, held-out units, and loss remain fixed. Thus the comparison asks whether shallow PCA compression improves prediction; it does not ask whether abstraction in general is useful.

The direct hypothesis predicts that the complete VALEX distribution improves on a training-frame-mean baseline for held-out verbs. The compression hypothesis predicts that the factor procedure improves on the direct procedure.

## Keeping every fitted choice inside training data

Five repetitions of ten-fold outer cross-validation hold out complete verbs. Within every outer training set, independent five-fold validation selects the direct ridge penalty and jointly selects factor rank and ridge penalty. Participant normalization, response aggregation, predictor centering, PCA loadings, rank, and penalty are refitted in the relevant training split.

Recall from the [cross-validation algorithm](../model-criticism-and-prediction/cross-validation.qmd#the-algorithm) that the complete fitting procedure must be rerun on each training fold before a prespecified loss is evaluated on its held-out units. Here the held-out unit is a verb and the outcome is its 50-cell response profile. No response for that verb enters normalization, aggregation, component estimation, or tuning. The participants themselves may occur in the training data through judgments of other verbs; the target is thus a new verb judged by the experiment's participant pool, rather than a simultaneously new verb and new participant.

The fixed candidate sets are:

```{r}
ridge_candidates <- c(0.01, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10) # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
rank_candidates <- c(2L, 5L, 10L, 20L, 30L, 40L, 50L) # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
```

The penalty grid spans nearly unpenalized through visibly regularized fits on the
training-centered scale. The rank grid is dense at low dimension and extends to
`r max(rank_candidates)`, equal to the `r length(unique(mega$frame))` response-frame targets; it tests substantial compression
without pretending to enumerate every possible rank. Outer folds hold out verbs
because the scientific target is a new lexical predicate, and every frame for a
verb moves with it. Five repetitions of ten-fold outer cross-validation reduce
dependence on one fold assignment while leaving about 90% of verbs for each fit.
Five inner folds provide a tractable repeated selection calculation inside each
outer training set.

Ties are resolved toward the larger ridge penalty, and factor ties then favor the
smaller rank, as the `order()` calls show. Five fixed outer seeds and their derived
inner seeds determine the random fold assignments before any response score is
compared.

The reported predictions come from one execution of this procedure in Python
with the five stated seeds. The R implementation below shows each operation:
fold construction, participant normalization, nested selection, and outer
prediction from the two inputs. Base R and NumPy use different seeded shuffling
algorithms, so running the R block follows the same procedure with different
fold assignments and may produce different numerical predictions. In either
implementation, response normalization, PCA, and tuning are recomputed within
the relevant training set.

```{r}
#| eval: false

make_folds <- function(indices, n_folds, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  shuffled <- sample(indices)
  labels <- rep(seq_len(n_folds), length.out = length(shuffled))
  lapply(seq_len(n_folds), function(fold) {
    test <- shuffled[labels == fold]
    list(training = setdiff(indices, test), test = test)
  })
}

population_sd <- function(x) {
  sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2))
}

build_outcome <- function(training_rows, responses, verbs, frames) {
  fitting <- responses$verb %in% verbs[training_rows]
  global_mean <- mean(responses$response[fitting])
  global_sd <- population_sd(responses$response[fitting])

  by_participant <- split(responses$response[fitting], responses$participant[fitting])
  participant_mean <- vapply(by_participant, mean, numeric(1))
  participant_sd <- vapply(by_participant, population_sd, numeric(1))

  row_mean <- participant_mean[as.character(responses$participant)]
  row_sd <- participant_sd[as.character(responses$participant)]
  fallback <- is.na(row_sd) | row_sd <= 1e-12
  row_mean[fallback] <- global_mean
  row_sd[fallback] <- global_sd
  responses$z <- (responses$response - row_mean) / row_sd

  cells <- aggregate(z ~ verb + frame, data = responses, FUN = mean)
  Y <- matrix(
    NA_real_, nrow = length(verbs), ncol = length(frames),
    dimnames = list(verbs, frames)
  )
  Y[cbind(match(cells$verb, verbs), match(cells$frame, frames))] <- cells$z
  stopifnot(!anyNA(Y))
  attr(Y, "normalization_audit") <- c(
    participants_without_training = sum(is.na(participant_sd)),
    participants_with_zero_training_sd = sum(participant_sd <= 1e-12)
  )
  Y
}

prepare_predictors <- function(P_training, P_test) {
  center <- colMeans(P_training)
  Z_training <- sweep(P_training, 2, center, "-")
  fit <- svd(Z_training)
  list(
    u = fit$u,
    d = fit$d,
    test_scores = sweep(P_test, 2, center, "-") %*% fit$v
  )
}

ridge_prediction <- function(prepared, Y_training, lambda, rank = NULL) {
  outcome_mean <- colMeans(Y_training)
  centered_outcome <- sweep(Y_training, 2, outcome_mean, "-")
  component_outcome <- crossprod(prepared$u, centered_outcome)
  if (is.null(rank)) rank <- length(prepared$d)
  rank <- min(rank, length(prepared$d))
  index <- seq_len(rank)
  shrinkage <- prepared$d[index] /
    (prepared$d[index]^2 + lambda)
  fitted_centered <- sweep(
    prepared$test_scores[, index, drop = FALSE],
    2, shrinkage, "*"
  ) %*% component_outcome[index, , drop = FALSE]
  sweep(fitted_centered, 2, outcome_mean, "+")
}

select_hyperparameters <- function(
  P, responses, verbs, frames, outer_training, seed,
  lambdas = ridge_candidates, ranks = rank_candidates,
  n_inner_folds = 5L
) {
  direct_sse <- setNames(rep(0, length(lambdas)), lambdas)
  factor_grid <- expand.grid(rank = ranks, lambda = lambdas)
  factor_grid$sse <- 0
  observations <- 0

  inner_partitions <- make_folds(
    outer_training, n_folds = n_inner_folds, seed = seed
  )
  for (inner in inner_partitions) {
    Y <- build_outcome(inner$training, responses, verbs, frames)
    prepared <- prepare_predictors(
      P[inner$training, , drop = FALSE],
      P[inner$test, , drop = FALSE]
    )
    Y_training <- Y[inner$training, , drop = FALSE]
    Y_validation <- Y[inner$test, , drop = FALSE]

    for (lambda in lambdas) {
      prediction <- ridge_prediction(prepared, Y_training, lambda)
      direct_sse[as.character(lambda)] <-
        direct_sse[as.character(lambda)] + sum((Y_validation - prediction)^2)
    }
    for (row in seq_len(nrow(factor_grid))) {
      prediction <- ridge_prediction(
        prepared, Y_training,
        factor_grid$lambda[[row]], factor_grid$rank[[row]]
      )
      factor_grid$sse[[row]] <- factor_grid$sse[[row]] +
        sum((Y_validation - prediction)^2)
    }
    observations <- observations + length(Y_validation)
  }

  direct_table <- data.frame(
    model = "direct", rank = ncol(P), lambda = lambdas,
    validation_mse = as.numeric(direct_sse) / observations
  )
  factor_table <- transform(
    factor_grid,
    model = "factor",
    validation_mse = sse / observations
  )[c("model", "rank", "lambda", "validation_mse")]

  direct_choice <- direct_table[
    order(direct_table$validation_mse, -direct_table$lambda)[[1]],
  ]
  factor_choice <- factor_table[
    order(
      factor_table$validation_mse,
      -factor_table$lambda,
      factor_table$rank
    )[[1]],
  ]
  list(
    direct_lambda = direct_choice$lambda,
    factor_rank = factor_choice$rank,
    factor_lambda = factor_choice$lambda,
    curves = rbind(direct_table, factor_table)
  )
}

run_nested_dsm <- function(
  P, responses, outer_seeds,
  n_outer_folds = 10L, n_inner_folds = 5L
) {
  verbs <- rownames(P)
  frames <- sort(unique(responses$frame))
  all_rows <- seq_len(nrow(P))
  prediction_list <- list()
  curve_list <- list()
  output_index <- 0L

  for (repeat_index in seq_along(outer_seeds)) {
    outer_folds <- make_folds(
      all_rows, n_folds = n_outer_folds, seed = outer_seeds[[repeat_index]]
    )
    for (fold_index in seq_along(outer_folds)) {
      fold <- outer_folds[[fold_index]]
      inner_seed <- outer_seeds[[repeat_index]] + 1000L * fold_index + 37L
      choice <- select_hyperparameters(
        P, responses, verbs, frames, fold$training, inner_seed,
        n_inner_folds = n_inner_folds
      )

      Y <- build_outcome(fold$training, responses, verbs, frames)
      prepared <- prepare_predictors(
        P[fold$training, , drop = FALSE],
        P[fold$test, , drop = FALSE]
      )
      Y_training <- Y[fold$training, , drop = FALSE]
      Y_test <- Y[fold$test, , drop = FALSE]
      baseline <- matrix(
        rep(colMeans(Y_training), each = length(fold$test)),
        nrow = length(fold$test)
      )
      direct <- ridge_prediction(
        prepared, Y_training, choice$direct_lambda
      )
      factor <- ridge_prediction(
        prepared, Y_training, choice$factor_lambda, choice$factor_rank
      )

      cells <- expand.grid(
        test_row = seq_along(fold$test),
        frame_column = seq_along(frames)
      )
      output_index <- output_index + 1L
      prediction_list[[output_index]] <- data.frame(
        `repeat` = repeat_index,
        fold = fold_index,
        verb = verbs[fold$test[cells$test_row]],
        frame = frames[cells$frame_column],
        outcome = Y_test[cbind(cells$test_row, cells$frame_column)],
        baseline = baseline[cbind(cells$test_row, cells$frame_column)],
        direct = direct[cbind(cells$test_row, cells$frame_column)],
        factor = factor[cbind(cells$test_row, cells$frame_column)]
      )
      choice$curves[["repeat"]] <- repeat_index
      choice$curves$outer_fold <- fold_index
      curve_list[[output_index]] <- choice$curves
    }
  }
  list(
    outer_predictions = do.call(rbind, prediction_list),
    inner_curves = do.call(rbind, curve_list)
  )
}

bootstrap_skill_by_verb <- function(predictions, seed, samples) {
  squared_error <- data.frame(
    verb = predictions$verb,
    baseline = (predictions$outcome - predictions$baseline)^2,
    direct = (predictions$outcome - predictions$direct)^2,
    factor = (predictions$outcome - predictions$factor)^2
  )
  by_verb <- aggregate(. ~ verb, data = squared_error, FUN = sum)
  set.seed(seed)
  draws <- replicate(samples, {
    rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(by_verb)), nrow(by_verb), replace = TRUE)
    denominator <- sum(by_verb$baseline[rows])
    direct <- 1 - sum(by_verb$direct[rows]) / denominator
    factor <- 1 - sum(by_verb$factor[rows]) / denominator
    c(direct = direct, factor = factor, difference = factor - direct)
  })
  t(apply(draws, 1, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975)))
}

outer_seeds <- c(4101L, 9777L, 203948L, 511903L, 884219L) # dqr-allow: random-seed
full_fit <- run_nested_dsm(P, mega, outer_seeds)
bootstrap_intervals <- bootstrap_skill_by_verb(
  full_fit$outer_predictions,
  seed = 731921L,
  samples = 5000L
)
```

Fitting one PCA to all verbs would create [leakage through preprocessing](../model-criticism-and-prediction/training-and-test-data.qmd#leakage-through-preprocessing), even though PCA does not use acceptability. The test verb's VALEX row is unavailable under the new-verb target and cannot determine its own component directions.

## Defining held-out skill

The baseline predicts the outer-training mean separately for each response frame. For model $m$, define

$$
R_m^2
=
1-
\frac{\sum_i(y_i-\widehat y_{m,i})^2}
     {\sum_i(y_i-\widehat y_{\mathrm{base},i})^2}.
$$

Positive values improve on the frame-mean baseline. The paired compression contrast is

$$
\Delta R^2
=
R_{\mathrm{factor}}^2-R_{\mathrm{direct}}^2.
$$

The uncertainty calculation resamples verbs, so each sampled unit carries every response frame and all repeated outer predictions for that verb.

```{r}
skill <- function(outcome, prediction, baseline) {
  1 - sum((outcome - prediction)^2) / sum((outcome - baseline)^2)
}

direct_skill <- skill(outer$outcome, outer$direct, outer$baseline)
factor_skill <- skill(outer$outcome, outer$factor, outer$baseline)

performance <- data.frame(
  representation = c("Direct VALEX profile", "PCA VALEX profile", "PCA minus direct"),
  skill = c(direct_skill, factor_skill, factor_skill - direct_skill),
  interval_low = c(
    pilot_summary$performance$bootstrap$direct$ci_low,
    pilot_summary$performance$bootstrap$factor$ci_low,
    pilot_summary$performance$bootstrap$delta$ci_low
  ),
  interval_high = c(
    pilot_summary$performance$bootstrap$direct$ci_high,
    pilot_summary$performance$bootstrap$factor$ci_high,
    pilot_summary$performance$bootstrap$delta$ci_high
  )
)
knitr::kable(performance, digits = 4)
```

The direct distribution achieves held-out skill `r round(direct_skill, 4)`, with a verb-bootstrap interval from `r round(performance$interval_low[[1]], 4)` to `r round(performance$interval_high[[1]], 4)`. The PCA procedure achieves `r round(factor_skill, 4)`. Its difference from the direct procedure is `r round(factor_skill - direct_skill, 4)`, and the paired interval lies below zero.

## Showing outcomes and held-out fits

Each verb-frame cell receives one prediction in every outer repetition. We average those five held-out predictions only for plotting.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7.4
#| fig-height: 4

cell_key <- paste(outer$verb, outer$frame, sep = "\r")
group <- match(cell_key, unique(cell_key))
cell_count <- tabulate(group)
cell_sums <- rowsum(
  as.matrix(outer[c("outcome", "direct", "factor")]),
  group = group,
  reorder = FALSE
)
cell_average <- sweep(cell_sums, 1, cell_count, "/")

plot_data <- rbind(
  data.frame(outcome = cell_average[, "outcome"],
             prediction = cell_average[, "direct"],
             model = "Direct VALEX profile"),
  data.frame(outcome = cell_average[, "outcome"],
             prediction = cell_average[, "factor"],
             model = "PCA VALEX profile")
)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = outcome, y = prediction)) +
  geom_bin_2d(bins = 35) + # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "white", linewidth = 0.45) +
  facet_wrap(~model) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "grey90", high = "#0072B2", name = "Cells") +
  labs(x = "Held-out normalized acceptability",
       y = "Held-out prediction") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank())
```

Both fitted procedures recover substantial ordering across held-out cells, though dispersion around the identity line remains. The panels are similar because PCA preserves much, but not all, of the direct predictive signal.

## Inspecting selected rank

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 3.8

factor_inner <- inner[inner$model == "factor", ]
best_penalty_within_rank <- aggregate(
  validation_mse ~ `repeat` + outer_fold + rank,
  data = factor_inner,
  FUN = min
)
rank_curve <- aggregate(
  validation_mse ~ rank,
  data = best_penalty_within_rank,
  FUN = mean
)
selected_ranks <- read.csv(
  file.path(analysis_root, "factor-selection-frequency.csv")
)
outer_fit_keys <- unique(inner[c("repeat", "outer_fold")])
selected_rank <- unique(selected_ranks$factor_rank)
stopifnot(
  length(selected_rank) == 1L,
  selected_rank == max(rank_candidates),
  sum(selected_ranks$outer_folds) == nrow(outer_fit_keys)
)

ggplot(rank_curve, aes(x = rank, y = validation_mse)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(color = "grey20", size = 1.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = selected_rank,
             color = "#0072B2", linewidth = 0.65) +
  labs(x = "Candidate PCA rank",
       y = "Mean inner-validation squared loss") +
  theme_classic()
```

Inner validation selects rank `r selected_rank`, the largest candidate, in all `r nrow(outer_fit_keys)` outer fits. This result does not identify that rank as the number of grammatical dimensions. It suggests that directions beyond the tested compression remain predictively useful.

## Locating the predictive limitation

White and Rawlins report a marked weakness for finite clauses preceded by a
direct object. We specified the corresponding frame-family comparison before
inspecting the results of the new procedure.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.2

family_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(family = family_metrics$family,
             representation = "Direct", skill = family_metrics$direct_skill),
  data.frame(family = family_metrics$family,
             representation = "PCA", skill = family_metrics$factor_skill)
)
family_long$family <- factor(
  family_long$family,
  levels = family_metrics$family[order(family_metrics$direct_skill)]
)

ggplot(family_long,
       aes(x = skill, y = family, shape = representation)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = family), color = "grey75", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(color = "grey20", size = 2) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Direct" = 16, "PCA" = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Held-out skill", y = "Frame family", shape = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

Direct skill for finite clauses without an object is `r round(family_metrics$direct_skill[family_metrics$family == "finite without object"], 3)`, but falls to `r round(family_metrics$direct_skill[family_metrics$family == "finite with direct object"], 3)` for the matched object frames. PCA does not repair this difference.

White and Rawlins connect the object pattern to communicativity: with a verb such as *persuade*, the object may denote a recipient of communicated content. The present prediction-error pattern is consistent with that proposal, though it cannot separate communicativity from animacy, discourse, polysemy, item construction, or corpus-analysis error.

## What the application establishes

First, automatically acquired VALEX distributions contain information about MegaAcceptability profiles for verbs excluded from fitting. Second, PCA compression does not improve that mapping: the selected factor procedure performs slightly and stably worse than the direct profile. The result counts against this shallow compression for this target, not against abstract syntactic or semantic representations in general.

The present analysis differs from the paper in three declared ways. We use raw VALEX proportions rather than the paper's best Beta Negative Binomial representation, PCA rather than a logistic factor model, and a fold-fitted z transformation rather than the released ordinal mixed-effects normalization. Holding the predictive target fixed lets us ask specifically what changes when PCA replaces the raw frame distribution.

## Checking the reasoning

1. What does one VALEX row represent, and which sense distinction does it omit?
2. Why are counts converted to within-verb proportions?
3. Why must participant normalization be refitted inside each split?
4. What is held constant between the direct and factor procedures?
5. Why does selecting the largest candidate rank not identify a grammatical dimensionality?
6. What does the negative compression contrast rule out, and what remains a live possibility?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. A VALEX row is a within-verb distribution of automatically acquired frame
   counts; it does not separate verb senses.
2. Proportions remove total count and target allocation across frames.
3. Using a test verb's responses to normalize its participants would leak target
   information into preprocessing.
4. Outcomes, held-out verbs, ridge family, and squared loss remain fixed.
5. It shows that the largest tested compression retained predictive value, not that
   grammar has fifty dimensions.
6. It counts against this shallow PCA compression for this held-out-verb target;
   theory-guided representations remain live possibilities.

</details>

## Recap

1. The data ladder runs from automatic VALEX counts and participant judgments to
   fold-normalized verb-by-frame targets.
2. Ridge follows from a penalized least-squares objective, and its SVD form exposes
   componentwise shrinkage.
3. Verb blocking and nested refitting keep every representational and tuning choice
   inside training data.

The live empirical question is which theory-guided representation of
communicativity, argument structure, or event structure can improve held-out
prediction without discarding the useful direct distributional signal.
